headlines.title: Gabby Williams scores 19 as Valkyries rally from 16 down to beat Wings 77-73, reach WNBA semifinals
headlines.description: Gabby Williams scored 19 points and hit a go-ahead 17-footer with 1:17 remaining, and the Golden State Valkyries won a late replay review to finish a rally from 16 points down and beat the Dallas Wings 77-73 on Friday night in a wild deciding Game 3 of their first-round WNBA playoff series. With 13.1 seconds left and Golden State leading by one, Williams jumped back inbounds to corral her own miss on a play that was originally ruled Dallas’ ball, but Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase — who moments earlier had fallen to her knees on the sideline before being helped up — successfully challenged the call. Nakase walked off the court escorted by a member of her staff after the final buzzer, holding her face as the team celebrated at midcourt. Arike Ogunbowale knocked down an off-balance jumper with 3:13 to play that put Dallas up by five and finished with 30 points to follow up a 45-point performance in the Wings’ overtime win Wednesday night at home. Williams scored all but two of her points after halftime. Veronica Burton had 16 points, 10 rebounds and six assists. Burton’s layup with 8:19 to play pulled the Valkyries within 61-59, Williams hit two 3-pointers late in the third and they both willed Golden State into the best-of-five semifinals against the defending WNBA champion Las Vegas Aces. Game 1 is Sunday at rocking Ballhalla with the team’s deafening, violet-crazed home crowd at Chase Center. Tiffany Hayes scored 18 points off the bench, Kaila Charles hit a tying 3-pointer with 6:51 left and Kiah Stokes pulled down 13 rebounds. The second-seeded Valkyries won a playoff series for the first time. Last year, they became the first expansion team to reach the playoffs in its inaugural season. Paige Bueckers had 17 points with six assists but shot only 3 for 14 for Dallas, making all 10 of her free throws. The Valkyries missed three straight 3s and nine shots in a row overall to start the third quarter as Dallas used a 9-0 run to take its largest lead at 53-37. Golden State pulled within 59-54 heading into the final 10 minutes. Ogunbowale was 11 for 21 after scoring a playoff-record 45 points in the Wings’ 108-100 overtime win Wednesday night. That prompted Nakase to declare before the game: “We made a promise to ourselves we are going to play the best four quarters of our lives.” She said the Valkyries didn’t recognize themselves that game — even though the team had scored 100 or more points in the first two matchups, including 104-80 in the series opener last Sunday. ___ AP WNBA: https://apnews.com/hub/wnba-basketball

headlines.title: 1 dead following multi-vehicle crash on I-80 in Berkeley
headlines.description: A deadly crash involving multiple vehicles on Interstate 80 in Berkeley is under investigation, according to the California Highway Patrol. The collision was reported just before 3:30 p.m. Friday and shut down several lanes on westbound I-80 near the University Avenue exit. At least five vehicles were involved in the collision and one person was pronounced dead at the scene, CHP said. There was no estimated time lanes would reopen and motorists were encouraged to use alternate routes. headlines.title: Man, woman dead after shooting at Oakland Hills home
headlines.description: A 61-year-old man and 63-year-old woman were found dead from apparent gunshot wounds outside their Oakland Hills home late Friday morning, according to police. Oakland and Berkeley police officers responded at about 10:45 a.m. to 499 Panoramic Way, not far from the University of California, Berkeley campus, to investigate reported gunshots, Oakland Police Department Assistant Chief Casey Johnson said. Officers found the man and woman suffering from apparent gunshot wounds outside the home. They both died at the scene, Johnson said. The man and woman appeared to be married and were residents at the home, according to Johnson. A firearm was recovered at the scene, Johnson said. It wasn’t immediately known if the shooting was a homicide or murder-suicide. “Everything’s a possibility until we can fully investigate this incident,” Johnson said. Johnson said there was no one in custody as of 1:30 p.m., adding that police were not looking for anyone at-large and that there was no threat to the surrounding neighborhood.

headlines.title: G7 nations will release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel fuel after prices soar
headlines.description: The Group of Seven wealthy democracies said Friday that they plan to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming weeks, starting with “substantial” amounts of diesel after the fuel recently hit record high prices in the United States. President Donald Trump said the diesel release would happen “immediately,” echoing a G7 promise to start “immediately” with a “frontloaded substantial release” of diesel within the next 20 days and the rest over four months. Trump and his Republican Party face pressure to address surging prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and Trump announced the action Friday on social media. The president’s approval ratings on the economy hit a new low, according to an AP-NORC poll, as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods. Gas prices in the U.S. and abroad have soared during the eight-month-long war, a cost Trump has repeatedly said is worth it for making sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was $6.37 on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22. Diesel prices have hit records in Europe, too. The release of diesel in Europe might mean less exports of diesel from the U.S., which could lower prices by 25-50 cents per gallon after a few weeks, said Michael Lynch, distinguished fellow at Energy Policy Research Foundation, a non-partisan research institution focused on energy and economics. Macron says the decision should bring down prices France holds the rotating presidency of the G7 group and made the announcement in a statement released after videoconference talks that Macron presided over. The G7 countries are Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the U.K. and the U.S., plus EU representation. The release follows on from a March announcement that International Energy Agency member countries would release 426 million barrels of oil and products to stabilize the oil market. European Union countries committed about 92 million barrels, a promise weighted toward refined products made from crude such as diesel. “This common decision and this unity should bring down prices,” Macron said. “The volumes we’re releasing should also add liquidity to the market and bring down prices.” In addition to the rise in the price of the crude oil from which diesel is made, other factors include the decision by Russia to ban exports due to Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries. Europe does not import Russian diesel, but other buyers of Russian diesel such as Turkey and Latin American countries must now compete with Europe for available barrels. Meanwhile refined product shipments from the Persian Gulf producers have fallen due to war damage and blocked export routes. The statement pushed U.S. oil prices down 2% but “the impact was lessened by lack of clarity on an important question,” said Pavel Molchanov, investment strategy analyst at Raymond James. Is the 100 million barrels in addition to the amount already agreed in March, or “is this the final portion of the existing pledge?” he said. The G7 says export bans are off the table Some Republicans in the U.S. had called for Trump to ban U.S. exports of diesel to try to bring domestic prices down. But the G7 statement said the group agreed not to limit energy exports to each other. Oil market analysts warn a U.S. export ban could lower prices in the short term but eventually backfire by reducing supplies of gasoline since diesel output can’t be lowered without also cutting overall refinery production. Asked about a potential U.S. export ban on Friday, Trump said “we were never going to do it.” “We’re not going to be doing the export ban,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “We’re going to be doing what we’re supposed to do.” He added that Europe is making “a major world contribution, and so are we.” Experts say there are risks in the strategy The emergency release could also be a short-term fix with the potential to do long-term harm, said Jim Krane, energy research fellow at Rice University’s Baker Institute. “Draining stocks will reduce retail fuel prices for a while, at the cost of leaving Europe with less emergency cover,” Krane said. “At some point in the future Europe and the rest of the G7 will have to refill their strategic reserves. Normally they try to do this when prices are low. Nobody knows when that will happen. It’s a risk.” With two wars raging that involve attacks on refineries and exports, “it’s not the best time to be frittering away your emergency stocks — especially when there is no visibility on future prices or peace agreements,” Krane said. Trump had a conversation overnight with Macron about the need to address rising fuel prices and the availability of petroleum products, according to the French Embassy in the U.S. Macron on Friday then chaired the videoconference of G7 leaders to discuss the issue. Besides his call with Macron, Trump on Friday called in to the meeting with the G7 leaders to negotiate the release of the European diesel stockpiles, according to a White House official who was not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity. Trump on Thursday embarked on what he said would be a 32-day marathon of rallies to try to bolster his party’s chances for keeping control of the U.S. House and Senate in the November elections. The president has grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a disconnect between his achievements and the public’s view of his work. This week he gave himself an A-plus for his work on the economy but said “we’re doing an extremely poor job of promotion.” ___ Leicester reported from Paris. AP writer Michelle L. Price contributed to this report. AP Business Writer David McHugh contributed from Frankfurt, Germany and Cathy Bussewitz contributed from New York.
headlines.source: COLLIN BINKLEY and JOHN LEICESTER | Associated Press

headlines.title: San Jose pantry using sidewalk to hand out food facing city code violations
headlines.description: A San Jose food pantry said it might have to close after the city gave it an order to stop handing out food because it is blocking parts of a public sidewalk. The Lighthouse Food Rescue on north 17th Street has been put on notice. Code enforcement sent the nonprofit an email saying its use of the sidewalk to distribute food does not comply with current zoning rules. The city also says the farmer’s market style setup obstructs a public sidewalk and has given lighthouse 60 days to cease operations. The Lighthouse already faced a battle with the city during the COVID-19 pandemic over permits. But this time, the nonprofit might be forced to close. Dennis Grijalva is one of those in line preparing hours before opening the food pantry. “I mean, food prices have gone up and up and up and up. People’s salaries haven’t really changed. And those who haven’t it’s not enough to compensate for people’s food need,” Grijalva said. “We’re in a strange time right now where we feel there’s all this red tape in our nonprofit world. And doing a good deed today is just not easy,” president and CEO Pastor Ralph Olmos said. Lighthouse says it will fight city hall. The nonprofit’s lawyer sent a letter to the director of code enforcement, demanding a sit-down meeting. “I’ve reached out to our Code department to see if we can provide an extension to Lighthouse as they work to find a new location,” said San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan. “My team is also working to connect the Pastor with potential partners who may be able to store their resources temporarily while they find a more permanent solution. While we have to follow the law and zoning designations, we can do it with care and find compromises.”

headlines.title: Oakland's Skyline High cancels football season early due to player availability
headlines.description: Skyline High in Oakland is ending its varsity football season early after the school says it no longer has enough players available. Skyline High is the second East Bay school in the past week to cancel its season, partly due to player safety. The first school was Mount Diablo High. The school was supposed to play against Benicia High, but Mount Diablo High canceled its varsity season last week amid player safety concerns. “We had to scramble to fill our spot today to have a homecoming game and we’ve heard of other schools having to do the same,” Benicia High principal Brianna Kleinschmidt said. Skyline High did the same. The storied Oakland program, once led by the late John Beam, is canceling its season, citing injuries, transfers and other circumstances impacting player availability. In a statement, the principal wrote, “This is a decision we do not take lightly and it came after exhausting all other options.” The news came as a shock to many in the McClymonds crowd, since the school has been rivals with Skyline over the years. “It’s a shock really, because when I was growing up Skyline was the dominant force,” parent Laron Blackwell said. Leia Grew, a parent, agrees that player safety comes first. Her son even chose to wear a “guardian cap” over his helmet as an added layer of protection. “He’s the only one on the team that has one. I’m really happy he has it on, we do a lot of stretching. I think player safety is of big importance,” she said. Some head trauma experts can’t say whether head-injury concerns are driving high school players away from football, but what has changed is awareness. “The awareness of head injuries have gone up. More parents are seeking care when their kid gets injured,” UCSF neurological surgery assistant professor Dr. John Yue said. Looking ahead, Skyline says it will spend the rest of the school year recruiting more student athletes, with the goal of rebuilding its football program for next season.

headlines.title: Sierra LaMar murder case: Judge will not recuse himself, jury selection next week
headlines.description: A judge announced Friday he will not recuse himself from a retrial for the man accused in the death of Morgan Hill teenager Sierra LaMar. Judge Brian Buckelew’s decision comes after he was called biased by the defense team for Antolin Garcia-Torres and moves the case forward. Friday’s court hearing also saw Buckelew rule on several pre-trial motions, including DNA experts allowed in the case. Garcia-Torres’s defense team previously argued the judge was biased based on a handful of prior rulings and because he used to work as a prosecutor in Santa Clara County. Buckelew decided not to step aside, citing he had no involvement in Garcia-Torres’s first case and the defense waited too long to object to him hearing the new case. The defense team did not challenge the judge’s decision. “This was a legal long shot for the defense to try to recuse a judge at this point in the trial and the judge was careful to make a very detailed record as to why this was not proper because this case may go up on appeal,” legal analyst Steven Clark said. “And he wants to have a very clear record of why he stayed in this case.” Morgan Hill Apr 27 Morgan Hill Mar 2 Morgan Hill Feb 27 After Buckelew denied the motion and the trial moved forward, the judge ruled prosecutors would not be able to use the DNA data firm from the first trial, Cybergenetics, for potential analysis. Buckelew cited a conflict of interest in his ruling. “The prosecution is going to have to rely on the forensic evidence and, now, we’re 14 years later and technology has changed so much,” Clark said. “And if they can’t use the most up-to-date DNA analyst and lab, that could severely affect their case because the defense will be ready to go on this issue.” The 15-year-old LaMar vanished in March 2012 while on her way to school in Morgan Hill and her body was never found. Her cell phone and belongings were later discovered on the side of the road two miles from her home, containing trace evidence that tied Garcia-Torres to her disappearance. Her DNA was also found in Garcia-Torres’s car. But without a body, murder weapon, or crime scene, that forensic DNA was the crux of the Santa Clara County District Attorney’s case. In June 2017, Garcia-Torres was sentenced to life for her murder. A judge in February overturned the conviction, partly because the district attorney had used three unrelated kidnapping cases to help convict Garcia-Torres. Garcia-Torres has remained in prison. The final stages of jury selection in the retrial is scheduled to resume next week.

headlines.title: Padilla pays unannounced visit to SFO's immigration holding facility
headlines.description: Sen. Alex Padilla of California made an impromptu visit to San Francisco International Airport’s immigration holding facility Thursday night in response to constituents’ concerns that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been using the facility more frequently in recent months at the direction of the Trump administration. Padilla said his visit to the Customs and Border Protection holding facility was part of an effort to achieve some transparency regarding increased operations by ICE agents at SFO. Padilla said he was greeted by a few uniformed Customs and Border Protection officers who ultimately toured him through the customs inspection areas. Padilla said there were less than 10 people at the immigration holding facility, but he did not know why they were there nor how long they had been there. Padilla said the holding area should not be used as a formal ICE facility. “There are certain standards that need to be met, and they’re sort of makeshift, trying to comply with,” Padilla said. “Not just access to restrooms and drinking water and food, but things like accommodations for folks that are being detained there to be able to communicate with their family or to communicate with their lawyer.” Concerns have been raised by immigration attorneys and family members over some people being held for days. In a statement, a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said the facilities at SFO offer appropriate accommodations, including access to medical services, if needed. “As part of the inspection process, certain travelers may require additional processing based on the circumstances of their case,” the statement read. “The length and nature of that processing can vary depending on a number of factors…” There has been increased attention on SFO’s immigration holding facility after two high-profile incidents this year in which ICE agents detained two different women who were traveling through the airport. NBC News reported that immigration agents in August increased the number of arrests and detentions at airports across the country. Padilla said visits like the one he made are part of a coordinated effort among some of his Democratic congressional colleagues to ensure the issue stays in the spotlight. “Because our Republican colleagues in Congress – they’re the majority – refuse to hold hearings in committee, to demand more information and answers from this administration,” Padilla said.

headlines.title: Marin County residents concerned after report reveals Flock cameras data breach
headlines.description: A North Bay newspaper says Flock cameras operated by the Marin County Sheriff’s Department were accessed thousands of times by out of state and federal agencies. Critics say that’s exactly the scenario they’ve been warning about. The Marin County Sheriff’s Office says its 31 Flock cameras have been a game-changing tool. But they acknowledge that, somehow, out-of-state agencies accessed data from the county’s cameras for nine weeks without the department’s permission. “I feel sad for our community. I definitely feel that our shared sense of safety and trust has eroded,” Tara Evans said. Evans was among three residents who sued and later reached a settlement with the county in 2022. “That case we actually found that the sheriff’s office was sharing driver license plate information out of state for the express purpose of assisting with federal immigration enforcement,” Nick Hildago with ACLU said. The Point Reyes Light newspaper discovered that multiple out-of-state agencies conducted more than 250,000 searches of Marin County’s camera data in late 2024. “It is a menace to the safety of California residents for the Marin sheriff to be violating state law and letting license plate reader data leave our state and go to federal and out of state police departments,” Adam Schwartz with Electronic Frontier Foundation said. The Marin County Sheriff’s Department acknowledged they learned in late 2024 that a breech had taken place for nine weeks without their knowledge in a statement that said, “upon discovering the issue, we again immediately deactivated the ability for out-of-state agencies to view our limited data.” The sheriff’s office says they are still waiting to hear from Flock why it happened, but says, “Protecting Marin County residents’ privacy is our responsibility, and we remain committed to transparency and accountability.” The Electronic Frontier Foundation and the ACLU have sent a letter to the department demanding answers. “We have no idea whether these were run to prosecute someone seeking an abortion to assist with ICE to track people who exercise their first amendment rights to protest or what have you. We just don’t know,” Hidalgo said. Evans says she’ll keep fighting to protect her community and says she’s considering filing another lawsuit.

headlines.title: 49ers owner Jed York suspended for 6 games after his arrest in prostitution sting
headlines.description: The NFL suspended San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York for six games Friday following his arrest earlier this year in a prostitution sting in Ohio. The league announced that York also was fined $500,000 for violating the league’s personal conduct policy. York has not attended any games or league meetings so far this season and was credited with three games served. He is eligible to return on Oct. 20, following the team’s game the previous night against Washington. The NFL’s fall league meetings begin that day in New York. York said in a statement released by the team that he accepts the punishment given by the league and apologized for his actions. “To my family, to the players, coaches, and employees of the San Francisco 49ers, to our fans and partners, I am deeply sorry,” he said. “This was an inexcusable mistake and I take full responsibility. What I did does not reflect my values or the man I strive to be for my family. While I fell short of the model I want to set for my sons, I now hope to show them the importance of owning up to one’s failures, and that even our worst moments teach us to be better. Leading the 49ers is a privilege, and one I don’t take lightly. Your trust will have to be earned back over time, and I look forward to that work ahead.” York was arrested in a mobile home park by the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force in August after police said he was attempting to pay $160 for sex with a woman he believed to be a prostitute. York was booked into jail and was released after posting a $5,000 bond. York was initially charged with engaging in prostitution, but prosecutors amended that to disorderly conduct. He pleaded no contest to that charge and to possessing criminal tools for using his phone to respond to an undercover online prostitution advertisement. He was sentenced to one day in jail for both offenses to be served concurrently and was credited with one day served when he pleaded no contest. He also was fined $1,150. Police seized the $160 from York and that was later given to the human trafficking task force as part of the plea. York also completed an online course. Owners have been previously punished for violating the personal conduct policy. The late Indianapolis Colts owner Jim Irsay was suspended for six games and fined $500,000 following a guilty plea to driving while impaired in 2014. New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft was investigated but not punished by the league after he was arrested in Florida in 2019 for allegedly paying for sex with a woman at a massage parlor. The charge was later dropped after a court ruled that police violated the rights of Kraft and the other customers when they secretly installed video cameras inside massage rooms at the spa. York spent most of the summer in Ohio, where he grew up near Youngstown and had been away from the team even before his arrest. He had filed for divorce from his wife, Danielle, in May, according to court records. York took over day-to-day control of the 49ers from his parents in 2008. He became the team’s principal owner in 2024. After some initial struggles under York’s leadership, the team has been a consistent contender since hiring coach Kyle Shanahan and general manager John Lynch in 2017. The Niners have made the Super Bowl three times under York’s leadership, losing in the 2012 season under coach Jim Harbaugh and the 2019 and ’23 seasons under Shanahan and Lynch. York also oversaw the building of Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara. The team moved from San Francisco to the new stadium in 2014. The stadium has hosted two Super Bowls, a World Cup and a College Football Playoff title game.

headlines.title: New museum tells the story of Dogpatch's industrial past
headlines.description: As San Francisco’s Dogpatch neighborhood undergoes a metamorphosis from gritty industrial hub to hip cutting-edge neighborhood, a new museum has popped up to remind the neighborhood of its past. The Pier 70 Time Machine sits tucked away on the second floor of newly restored Building 12 at Pier 70, where legions of workers once built Navy destroyers during World War II — but now houses a scooter business, padel courts, a brewery and other businesses. The museum was opened by Peter Linenthal and Bill Perez, two historians who merged their collections of ephemera to tell the history of the area’s shipbuilding along with the stories of nearby neighborhoods of Potrero Hill, Mission Bay and the now-gone Irish Hill. “People don’t know that where we are in Dogpatch was an industrial hub that shortly after the founding of San Francisco, that really built the city that we know today,” said Linenthal, who runs the Potrero Archives Project. The 4,000-square-foot museum is filled with pieces of industrial past, such as a room devoted to the tools used in shipbuilding. Perez, who once worked in Bethlehem Steel — the massive shipbuilding operation that supplied military ships during World War II — is now president of the Bethlehem Shipyard Museum. Before opening the new museum, his collection of industrial items filled his garage. Similarly, Linenthal stored his collection of items telling the stories of the nearby neighborhoods, with hopes of one day having a place to show it all. “It’s really a dream come true to have a space like this where we can share our collections for free with the public,” Linenthal said. Linenthal pointed out an old-time dentist chair that once belonged to Potrero Hill dentist Dr. Jean Pierre Cantou, who operated in the neighborhood between the 1930s and the 1960s. Nearby sat a replica of a tule boat that would’ve been used by Ramaytush Ohlone indigenous tribes that once inhabited Potrero Point more than 1,000 years before the arrival of the gold miners. Linenthal pointed out a large, glowing-red beacon that once sat atop a huge gas tank located near present-day Pennsylvania and Cesar Chavez streets. “We’re telling the stories of the people that worked in those industries, in the development of those industries,” said Linenthal. “And actually we’re going back to tell the story of the native people who lived here thousands of years ago.” Admission to the museum is free — it’s open Fridays from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. and Saturdays from noon to 4 p.m. The museum’s founders plan to expand their offerings to include more interactive exhibits to further interest young people in the neighborhood’s many stories. “One of our goals is to become a cultural hub,” said Perez. The museum also tells the story of Wendy the Welder, a counterpart to the famous Rosie the Riveter icon that paid tribute to women who worked in the shipyards. Another exhibit pays tribute to Irish Hill, the one-time working-class neighborhood that existed on a nearby hill that is no longer there. As Dogpatch and the Pier 70 area undergo a massive revamp, Linenthal hopes the museum will inform people of the origins of the brick buildings and metal barns that once were home base to a thriving industrial machine. “Things are changing so quickly that I think it’s important to look at the past just to understand all the changes the city has been through before,” Linenthal said.
